issues.subcategory: contradictory SESOI values
issues.description: The equivalence region is stated as δ = .27 in one paragraph and then justified and restated as δ = |.11| several paragraphs later. The initial statement says 'equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27' but the detailed justification concludes 'setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.' These cannot both be correct, and it is unclear which value will actually be used for the equivalence tests, which is central to the study's ability to test hypotheses 2b and 3b.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent Cohen's d values for same effect
issues.description: The same effect from Grubbs, Lee, et al. (2020) with ΔR² = .012 and f² = .016 is reported with Cohen's d = .22 in the initial listing of effect sizes and then as Cohen's d = .25 later in the detailed justification of the SESOI. These refer to the same source and the same analysis but report different effect size conversions.
issues.quote: small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring mismatch between text and supplement
issues.description: The methods section states the PGSI uses 'a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always),' which matches the standard validated scoring. However, the supplemental materials show the response options coded as Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5), which is a completely different and non-standard scoring scheme. This discrepancy would fundamentally affect the psychometric properties of the measure and makes it unclear what scoring will actually be implemented.
issues.quote: on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring mismatch between text and supplement
issues.description: The methods section describes the Brief Pornography Screen as using 'a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.' However, the supplemental materials show the response options coded as Never (0), Occasionally (2), Very Often (4). The supplemental scoring (0, 2, 4) does not match the validated scoring (0, 1, 2) described in the text.
issues.quote: on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency scale inconsistency
issues.description: The methods section describes pornography frequency as measured 'on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day),' but the substance use measures describe the same scale type as '0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day).' The supplemental materials confirm the 0-5 coding. The pornography section appears to use 1-6 coding while everything else uses 0-5, which would create non-parallel measures despite the stated goal of parallel assessment.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)

issues.subcategory: moral incongruence redefined mid-text as severity of consequences
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, moral incongruence is consistently defined as the interaction of moral disapproval and behavioral frequency. However, in the Present Study section, the authors state it is 'the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.' This contradicts the operational definition used everywhere else in the paper and appears to be an error or leftover from a previous draft.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: number of moderation analyses unclear
issues.description: The analytic plan states 'we will conduct 8 moderation analyses,' but only 7 target behaviors are listed (alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, pornography, and gambling). While Table 1 notes that pornography and gambling each have two outcome measures (validated scale + NIDA-ASSIST), it is not clearly specified which combination yields exactly 8 analyses, and whether NIDA-ASSIST versions for pornography and/or gambling are included as separate primary analyses.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: criterion contamination in BPS
issues.description: Item 5 of the Brief Pornography Screen reads 'You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.' Guilt about pornography use is conceptually and empirically related to moral disapproval of pornography (a key predictor in the model). This means the dependent variable partially captures moral distress, which could artifactually inflate the observed interaction effect for pornography relative to other behaviors whose outcome measures (NIDA-ASSIST, PGSI) do not include guilt items. This systematic measurement asymmetry could produce the hypothesized pattern of results (moral incongruence predicting pornography problems but not substance/gambling problems) as a measurement artifact rather than a true difference.
issues.quote: 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: measurement asymmetry across behaviors
issues.description: Pornography and gambling have validated, behavior-specific outcome measures (BPS and PGSI), while all five substance categories rely on modified NIDA-ASSIST items that have not been validated in their modified form. This measurement asymmetry means differences in moral incongruence effects across behaviors could reflect differences in measurement sensitivity, reliability, or construct coverage rather than true differences in the role of moral incongruence. The study's central comparison—whether moral incongruence uniquely predicts pornography problems—is undermined by this non-equivalence.
issues.quote: In addition to the modified NIDA-ASSIST items listed above, self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be assessed using the Brief Pornography Screen

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval may not be equivalent across behaviors
issues.description: The construct of 'moral disapproval' likely differs qualitatively across behaviors. Moral disapproval of pornography is often rooted in religious or sexual values, while moral disapproval of substance use may reflect stigma, health concerns, or legal perceptions. Using identically-worded single items ('I believe that using ___ is morally wrong') assumes construct equivalence across domains, but participants may interpret 'morally wrong' differently for sexual behaviors versus substance use, undermining the comparability of interaction effects.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement "I believe that using ________ is morally wrong" on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: sports-betting oversample biases gambling analyses
issues.description: The sample includes a 1,500-person oversample of sports bettors recruited specifically for the parent study. Table 2 shows that this oversample is included in the gambling analyses (effective N = 3,325, including 100% of the oversample). This creates a non-representative gambling subsample with overrepresentation of sports bettors, who may differ systematically from other gamblers in moral attitudes, gambling frequency, and problem severity. This biased composition could affect the generalizability of gambling-specific results and the comparison with pornography findings.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically

issues.subcategory: NIDA-ASSIST averaging items on different scales
issues.description: The analytic plan proposes averaging five NIDA-ASSIST items to create a composite problematic use score, but three items use a 0-5 frequency scale while two items use a 0/3/6 response scale. Simple averaging without standardization gives disproportionate weight to the two items with a larger range (0-6), distorting the composite. This could affect the sensitivity and construct coverage of the dependent variable for substance use analyses.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest

issues.subcategory: temporal mismatch across measures
issues.description: The frequency measures assess past 12-month behavior, the BPS assesses past 6-month experiences, and the NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items assess past 3-month experiences. This temporal mismatch means that the predictor (annual frequency) and outcome (recent problems) reference different time periods, which could attenuate associations or introduce systematic error, particularly for behaviors with variable frequency over time.
issues.quote: participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months

issues.subcategory: no correction for multiple comparisons across primary hypotheses
issues.description: Eight moderation analyses are planned as primary tests, but no correction for multiple comparisons is specified for these focal analyses. The Holm correction is mentioned only for bivariate correlations. With 8 interaction tests, the family-wise error rate is substantially inflated, which is particularly concerning when some tests use NHST (pornography) and others use equivalence testing (substances/gambling), making the overall error control framework unclear.
issues.quote: As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software, followed by equivalence tests

issues.subcategory: asymmetric statistical frameworks across behaviors
issues.description: For pornography, the hypothesis is tested using traditional NHST (expecting a significant interaction), while for gambling and substances, equivalence testing is used (expecting the interaction to fall within the equivalence interval). These are fundamentally different statistical frameworks with different error rates and evidential standards, making direct comparison across behaviors problematic. A unified framework (e.g., equivalence testing for all behaviors, or comparing confidence intervals across behaviors) would provide a more rigorous comparison.
issues.quote: we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software, followed by equivalence tests using the reg.equiv.fd function

issues.subcategory: insufficient power for key analyses
issues.description: Table 2 shows estimated achieved power of .301 for prescription drug misuse and .472-.764 for illicit substances at the target effect size. This means the study is substantially underpowered to test its hypotheses for two of the seven target behaviors. While the authors propose an alternative analysis with a wider equivalence region, this alternative tests a different (and weaker) hypothesis than the primary one, undermining the study's ability to draw conclusions about moral incongruence for these substances.
issues.quote: Prescription Drug Misuse | 3.5% | 140 | .057 | .301

issues.subcategory: unvalidated modifications to NIDA-ASSIST
issues.description: The NIDA-ASSIST has been substantially modified: response scales have been changed (adding 'more than once per day'), new behaviors have been added (pornography, gambling), and the instrument is used outside its validated context. These modifications may alter the psychometric properties of the instrument. The authors acknowledge this for pornography/gambling ('such an approach is not currently validated') but do not address the impact of scale modifications on other substances.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency limited to solo use
issues.description: The supplemental materials reveal that pornography frequency is assessed only for viewing 'alone (i.e., without a partner),' excluding partnered pornography use. This restriction is not mentioned or justified in the methods text and is inconsistent with the broad definition of pornography provided to participants. It could underestimate frequency for some participants and affect the interaction term.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional design
issues.description: Despite acknowledging the cross-sectional nature of the study as a limitation, the introduction and hypotheses repeatedly use causal or directional language (e.g., 'moral incongruence predicts,' 'moral disapproval amplifies,' 'moral incongruence is a clear contributor to'). Cross-sectional interaction effects cannot establish temporal ordering or causation. People who perceive themselves as addicted may subsequently develop moral disapproval, reversing the assumed causal direction.
issues.quote: moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction to, compulsivity in, or problems with pornography use

issues.subcategory: confirmatory framing rather than objective testing
issues.description: The stated goal is to 'demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors' rather than to objectively test whether it is unique. This confirmatory framing, combined with the asymmetric statistical approach (NHST for pornography, equivalence testing for others) and measurement advantages for pornography (validated BPS with guilt item), suggests the design is structured to confirm rather than rigorously test the hypothesis.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors

issues.subcategory: fallback equivalence region introduces researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: The analytic plan includes a primary SESOI (which itself is unclear due to the .27 vs .11 discrepancy) and a fallback equivalence region based on the lower bound of the 95% CI for the pornography interaction effect. This fallback creates a conditional analytic path where the equivalence region used depends on the obtained data, introducing a researcher degree of freedom. The decision criterion for when to switch from the primary to the fallback analysis is not fully pre-specified beyond the effects 'exceeding the region of equivalence.'
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence

issues.subcategory: underspecified robustness check procedures
issues.description: The analytic plan states that when regression assumptions are violated, 'we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.' The specific alternative methods are not pre-specified, creating analytic flexibility. Given that outcomes for rare behaviors (prescription drugs, illicit drugs) will likely have heavily zero-inflated, non-normal distributions, assumption violations are highly probable, and the choice of alternative analysis could meaningfully affect results.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate

issues.subcategory: power analysis for equivalence tests not reported
issues.description: Table 2 reports power to detect effects using standard regression power analysis (NHST framework), but the primary inferential tool for most hypotheses is equivalence testing, which has different power requirements. Power for equivalence tests depends on the SESOI, true effect size, and sample size in a way that differs from NHST power. No equivalence-specific power analysis is reported, making it unclear whether the study is adequately powered to demonstrate equivalence for the behaviors where this is hypothesized.
issues.quote: Estimated Achieved power for f2= .015

issues.subcategory: no contingency plan for missing data
issues.description: The authors assume no unplanned missingness based on YouGov's proprietary data collection standards, but provide no contingency plan if this assumption is violated. No missing data handling strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation) is pre-specified. Given that problematic use measures are administered only to users of each substance, differential nonresponse across substances could introduce systematic bias.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: gambling prevalence estimate likely inflated by broad definition
issues.description: The 73% gambling prevalence estimate used for power calculations likely reflects the very broad definition of gambling that includes buying lottery tickets. This means the 'gambling' subsample will be dominated by occasional lottery purchasers who are unlikely to experience gambling problems, creating a highly skewed and heterogeneous sample. The moral incongruence effect for gambling may be diluted by this composition, potentially creating a false negative for gambling that artificially supports the uniqueness hypothesis for pornography.
issues.quote: Gambling | 73% (national sample) 100% (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: gender operationalized as binary
issues.description: The analytic plan codes gender as 'binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male,' collapsing all non-male identities into a single category. This approach may not adequately represent gender diversity and could introduce measurement error. Additionally, it is unclear whether YouGov's panel data includes non-binary gender options, meaning the operationalization may not match the data collected.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: interaction term as proxy for experienced incongruence
issues.description: The operationalization of moral incongruence as a statistical interaction (moral disapproval × frequency) is a proxy for the psychological experience of incongruence between values and behavior. An individual could score high on both moral disapproval and frequency without subjectively experiencing incongruence (e.g., through compartmentalization), or could experience profound incongruence with infrequent behavior. The interaction term captures statistical moderation but may not validly represent the phenomenological construct of moral incongruence as described in the theoretical framework.
issues.quote: more recent work posits that moral incongruence is better conceptualized as the interaction of moral disapproval and use, rather than simply as the presence of moral disapproval among users

issues.subcategory: religiousness composite construction underspecified
issues.description: The three religiousness items from Pew have different response scales (importance: 4-point; prayer frequency: 7-point; attendance: multiple categories). The authors state these will be standardized and averaged, then multiplied by -1. However, the standardization method is not specified (z-scoring, min-max, etc.), and the equal weighting of these three conceptually different dimensions (salience, private practice, public practice) is not justified. The psychometric properties of this ad-hoc composite are unknown.
issues.quote: Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items taken from Pew Research Center

issues.subcategory: base rate differences across behaviors confound comparison
issues.description: Moral disapproval is not equally distributed across behaviors. Most people do not morally disapprove of alcohol use, but many morally disapprove of illicit drug use or pornography. These base rate differences in moral disapproval mean that the variance and distribution of the moral disapproval variable will differ dramatically across behaviors, potentially making interactions detectable for some behaviors (where there is sufficient variance in disapproval) but not others (where disapproval has restricted range). The authors do not discuss how these distributional differences could affect the comparability of interaction effects.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral incongruence regarding pornography use will predict self-reported feelings of addiction.

issues.subcategory: no attention checks or validity indicators planned
issues.description: The authors rely entirely on YouGov's proprietary quality control with no study-specific attention checks, validity indicators, or consistency items. For a survey covering sensitive topics (sexual behavior, substance use, morality), this is a notable omission. Social desirability responding, which is likely correlated with moral conservatism, is not measured or controlled for despite being a plausible confound.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards
